candidates.quote: Days and months are travellers of eternity. So are the years that pass by.
candidates.author: Matsuo Bashō
candidates.work: The Narrow Road to the Deep North
candidates.locator: Opening sentence of the work; The Narrow Road to the Deep North and Other Travel Sketches, Penguin Classics, 1966
candidates.whyThisMonth: The first sentence of the most famous journey in Japanese letters makes time itself a traveller, so a new year is simply the road going on.

candidates.quote: Listen to the reed how it tells a tale, complaining of separations.
candidates.author: Rumi
candidates.locator: Book I, line 1 (the Song of the Reed); Nicholson, The Mathnawí of Jalálu’ddín Rúmí, vol. II, 1926; Nicholson ends the line with a dash
candidates.whyThisMonth: The opening line of the Masnavi begins with an instruction to listen, and its reed longs to return to where it started: a beginning made out of homesickness.

candidates.quote: In a hole in the ground there lived a hobbit.
candidates.author: J. R. R. Tolkien
candidates.whyThisMonth: The plainest first sentence in the language promises a whole world from one small, comfortable fact, which is how most good beginnings look at six in the morning.

candidates.quote: Now is the winter of our discontent made glorious summer by this sun of York.
candidates.author: William Shakespeare
candidates.locator: Act 1, scene 1, lines 1–2 (Richard, Duke of Gloucester); the speaker is the villain and the note must say so
candidates.whyThisMonth: The play’s first two lines turn a winter into a summer in one breath, a January sentence even though the man saying it is about to misuse it.
candidates.speaker: Richard, Duke of Gloucester

candidates.quote: We shall not cease from exploration, and the end of all our exploring will be to arrive where we started and know the place for the first time.
candidates.author: T. S. Eliot
candidates.locator: ‘Little Gidding’, part V; the four verse lines run on as one sentence
candidates.whyThisMonth: The best-known lines of the Quartets say that beginning again is not repetition but return, and that the familiar place is the one still to be discovered.

candidates.quote: And now let us believe in a long year that is given to us, new, untouched, full of things that have never been, full of work that has never been done, full of tasks, claims, and demands; and let us see that we learn to take it without letting fall too much of what it has to bestow upon those who demand of it necessary, serious, and great things.
candidates.author: Rainer Maria Rilke
candidates.locator: Letter to Clara Rilke, Capri, 1 January 1907; Norton, 1945, p. 253; the CFL wording ‘And now we welcome the new year’ is a paraphrase, this is the published sentence
candidates.whyThisMonth: Written on a New Year’s morning, it asks nothing of the year but belief in it, and asks of us only that we learn to take what it brings.
candidates.translator: Jane Bannard Greene and M. D. Herter Norton, 1945

candidates.quote: I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived.
candidates.author: Henry David Thoreau
candidates.locator: Ch. 2, ‘Where I Lived, and What I Lived For’
candidates.whyThisMonth: The sentence Walden is known by is a man explaining why he started over, and the word that carries it is deliberately.

candidates.quote: I am large, I contain multitudes.
candidates.author: Walt Whitman
candidates.locator: ‘Song of Myself’, section 51; the line sits in parentheses after ‘Do I contradict myself? Very well then I contradict myself’
candidates.whyThisMonth: Permission to contradict last year’s self is the whole of beginning again, and Whitman grants it in six words.

candidates.quote: A classic is a book that has never finished saying what it has to say.
candidates.author: Italo Calvino
candidates.locator: Definition 6 of the essay; The Uses of Literature, Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1986
candidates.whyThisMonth: For a year called The Classics it is the founding sentence: a book worth opening again is one that is not done with you.

candidates.quote: Our battered suitcases were piled on the sidewalk again; we had longer ways to go. But no matter, the road is life.
candidates.author: Jack Kerouac
candidates.whyThisMonth: The word that matters is again: the suitcases are back on the pavement and the sentence still ends in cheer.
candidates.speaker: Sal Paradise (narrator)

candidates.quote: And, when you want something, all the universe conspires in helping you to achieve it.
candidates.author: Paulo Coelho
candidates.locator: Part One (Melchizedek, the king of Salem, to Santiago); HarperCollins, 1993
candidates.whyThisMonth: The sentence the novel is known by is said to a boy at the very start of his journey, which is where a January reader is standing.
candidates.speaker: Melchizedek, the king of Salem

candidates.quote: yes I said yes I will Yes.
candidates.author: James Joyce
candidates.locator: Episode 18, ‘Penelope’, final words (Molly Bloom); the 1922 text runs ‘and yes I said yes I will Yes.’
candidates.whyThisMonth: The most famous last word in the novel is an unconditional yes, and a book that ends there hands its reader a beginning.
candidates.speaker: Molly Bloom

candidates.quote: The only true voyage of discovery, the only fountain of Eternal Youth, would be not to visit strange lands but to possess other eyes.
candidates.author: Marcel Proust
candidates.locator: Ch. 2, the Vinteuil septet at the Verdurins’ (the narrator); the sentence continues; CFL’s ‘new eyes’ wording is a paraphrase, this is Moncrieff’s
candidates.whyThisMonth: Beginning again does not require a new place, only new eyes on the old one, and Proust says so about a piece of music, not a journey.
candidates.speaker: the narrator

candidates.quote: Light, my light, the world-filling light, the eye-kissing light, heart-sweetening light!
candidates.author: Rabindranath Tagore
candidates.locator: Poem 57, first line; Macmillan, 1912, in the author’s own English
candidates.whyThisMonth: A first line that is nothing but morning light, for the hour when the reader is waiting for exactly that.

candidates.quote: One cannot think well, love well, sleep well, if one has not dined well.
candidates.author: Virginia Woolf
candidates.locator: Ch. 1; theme fit is honest but thin, offered because CFL carries only two women
candidates.whyThisMonth: A day begun properly begins at the table, and Woolf puts the body before the resolutions.

candidates.quote: But man is not made for defeat. A man can be destroyed but not defeated.
candidates.author: Ernest Hemingway
candidates.work: The Old Man and the Sea
candidates.locator: Unchaptered; spoken aloud by Santiago after the first shark takes from the marlin
candidates.whyThisMonth: For the reader beginning again after a year that went badly, the old man’s line is the plain refusal to count a loss as an ending.
candidates.speaker: Santiago
